rounds.text: Tilak Ventures Ltd is significantly under-appreciated by the market, trading at an attractive price-to-book ratio of 0.91x against a sector benchmark of 1.29x [E7], and an EV/EBITDA of 12.5x compared to the sector benchmark of 13.32x [E11]. The underlying business exhibits explosive top-and-bottom-line expansion, demonstrated by a 3-year compounded sales growth of 90% [E14] and a staggering 3-year compounded profit growth of 162% [E16]. This operational momentum is underpinned by strong fundamental safety, highlighted by a pristine debt-to-equity ratio of just 0.06x [E30] and an exceptionally comfortable current ratio of 17.54x [E31]. Furthermore, insiders and leadership express immense confidence in the company's trajectory, with promoter holding increasing significantly from 55.62% in September 2023 to 61.98% in June 2026 [E34]. Valuation models reinforce this disconnect, as a discounted cash flow analysis estimates intrinsic value at Rs 2 per share against a market price of only Rs 1.30, providing a healthy margin of safety of 30.7% [E36, E37]. Conceded: the company carries a low return on equity of around 6% [E45, E53] and has failed to reward shareholders with dividends [E4, E44].

Despite headline top-line growth figures, Tilak Ventures Ltd suffers from persistent share price decay, with compounded share price growth contracting by 26% over 1 year, 10% over 3 years, and 23% over 5 years [E18, E19, E20]. Profitability metrics are deeply uninspiring, highlighted by a low 3-year median return on equity of 6% [E21] and a current ROE of 5.8% [E13], which aligns with the negative flag noting a low 3-year average ROE of 5.67% [E45]. Furthermore, earnings quality is highly questionable given that the cash conversion ratio sits at just 0.27x for March 2025, demonstrating that reported profits are running far ahead of actual cash generation due to potential receivables or accruals issues [E27]. Operational consistency is another major concern, as yearly and quarterly operating margins are explicitly characterized as inconsistent [E25, E26], underscored by a sharp quarterly margin contraction of 58 percentage points down to 18% in March 2025 compared to the same period a year ago [E24]. Compounding these operational hurdles, the company carries zero dividend yield [E4] and has been flagged for failing to pay out dividends despite reporting repeated profits [E44], while total borrowings have simultaneously surged from Rs 2.40 Cr to Rs 8.02 Cr over a single year [E32]. Conceded: [E14], [E15], [E16], [E34].

While the bear points to historical share price decay [E18, E19, E20], the business is actually starting to outperform expectations as profit growth now exceeds 1-year price growth by 43% [E40]. On valuation and operational comparisons, the company's price-to-book ratio of 0.91x sits below the sector benchmark of 1.29x [E7], and its EV/EBITDA of 12.5x also undercuts the sector benchmark of 13.32x [E11]. Addressing the concern over low ROE [E21, E13, E45], its return on assets of 4.25% actually outperforms the sector benchmark of 1.89% [E8]. Conceded: [E27], [E25], [E26], [E4], [E44], [E32]. Despite the noted surge in borrowings [E32], the company remains conservatively financed with a very low debt-to-equity ratio of 0.06x [E30], and management's commitment is evident as promoters have increased their holding to 61.98% as of June 2026 compared to 55.62% in September 2023 [E34]. Finally, the DCF model calculates an intrinsic value of Rs 2 per share offering a 30.7% margin of safety against the current market price of Rs 1.3 [E36, E37], while the reverse DCF indicates that today's price implies a modest 12.9% earnings growth compared to the 18.0% base case assumption [E38].

Conceded: [E7], [E11], [E8], and [E34]. The bull points to low valuation ratios like P/B and EV/EBITDA, but ignores that the company trades at a higher P/E of 20.14x against its sector benchmark of 18.87x [E6], as well as a standalone P/E of 27.9 [E1]. The claim that profit growth is starting to outperform expectations [E40] contradicts screened evidence that net profit fell 35% year-over-year and earnings growth is decelerating [E51, E52]. While the bull highlights the low debt-to-equity ratio [E30], it glosses over the fact that borrowings more than tripled to Rs 8.02 Cr in Mar 2025 from Rs 2.40 Cr a year prior [E32]. Furthermore, the reliance on DCF intrinsic value and margin of safety figures [E36, E37, E38] does nothing to erase a long-term pattern of wealth destruction, evidenced by compounded share price growth of -23% over 5 years, -10% over 3 years, and -26% over 1 year [E18, E19, E20].
